# Network Services 3

UK public sector organisations can access network solutions and communication services. This includes cloud connectivity, audio and video conferencing, radio and satellite networking, and emerging technologies like Smart Cities. 

## Updates

**15 August 2025:** This framework was set up under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015. These rules still apply for the full agreement. Both buying methods (further competition and direct award) remain available, even though the Procurement Act 2023 is now in effect.

**12 March 2025:** We have extended the length of this agreement by 24 months. The new end date is 17 July 2027. The new end date for lots 1c and 1d is 22 May 2027.

**19 September 2024:** If you are buying connectivity services under lot 1a or 2a we have a new template and guidance video to help define your requirements:

*   [connectivity in a box template document This file will download](https://assets.crowncommercial.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/Connectivity-In-A-Box-Template-v3-1.ods)
*   [connectivity in a box guidance video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZQT815Vf7-M)

**20 September 2023:** Mobile voice and data services are no longer part of this framework. Use the new [RM6261 Mobile Voice and Data Services Framework instead.](https://www.gca.gov.uk/agreements/RM6261)

**28 July 2023:**[Watch our RM6116 customer webinar.](https://youtu.be/NjFoaPzUZBU) It provides information on:

*   framework overview
*   buying process (direct award and further competition)
*   terms and conditions and service offers

## Description

Provides you with the flexibility to update, improve or simplify your network systems. Services and products you can buy include:

*   **routers, switches and cables:** equipment which allows network access
*   **local area networks:** equipment which allows connectivity within your organisation’s premises
*   internet access and fibre optic cabling
*   5G networks
*   **Internet Protocol (IP) telephony:** voice calls over the internet
*   **cloud services:**internet-based computing such as servers, storage and databases
*   **collaboration solutions:** audio and video conferencing
*   **unified communications:** platforms or applications that combine communication methods including voice, video and data services
*   **satellite networking:** wireless communication that uses satellites to send data and provide internet connectivity
*   maintenance and support services
*   **contact centre services:** software that connects many communication channels such as voice, email, chat and social media into a single unified system
*   security and surveillance
*   **professional services:** design, install and manage network solutions

### **Emerging technologies**

The agreement also includes access to newer technologies:

*   Internet of Things (IoT) and Smart Technologies (smart, shared, connected spaces)
*   tactical radio services (secure communication systems in high-risk unpredictable environments)
*   critical domain services (register and manage domain names)
*   communication platform as a service (embed real-time communication features into your own systems)

You can buy complete managed solutions from a single supplier. Or you can buy individual parts as needed. This helps you modernise, optimise, and simplify your network for hybrid working.

### **Agreement length**

Network services 3 will run for 2 years, with 2 optional 12-month extensions.

## Benefits

*   provides a complete range of network services from network infrastructure to fully integrated communication suites
*   introduces emerging technologies that reflect changes in the marketplace and future consumption of network solutions
*   supports the government’s “cloud first” initiatives aimed at enabling public internet connectivity solutions, and migration off the Public Sector Network (PSN)
*   attracts solution providers, service integrators and managed service providers who can remove the complexity of design from the end-user, and design, build and deliver solutions that provide cost and network optimisation
*   providing a WAN/LAN RFQ template to enable more “further competition” on public internet connectivity solutions and ultimately provide customers with better value for money
*   enabling direct awards on all Lots for commoditised procurements
*   enabling cross-lot competitions where managed services span across more than one capability

### Carbon Reduction

All suppliers have committed to comply with Procurement Policy Note 006, ['Taking account of Carbon Reduction Plans in the procurement of major government contracts'](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ppn-006-taking-account-of-carbon-reduction-plans-in-the-procurement-of-major-government-contracts) as required. If a supplier is required to publish a carbon reduction plan, you can find it on their individual supplier details page.

## Products and suppliers

There are [131 suppliers](https://www.gca.gov.uk/agreements/RM6116/suppliers) on this agreement

Lot 1a: Inter Site Connectivity (Wider Area Network) / Data Access Services

Connectivity services that link your sites together or connect your sites to the cloud. This includes:
*   terrestrial, fibre, wireless and satellite solutions
*   5G and 6G networks
*   data networking equipment
*   software defined WAN, Secure Access Service Edge (SASE)
*   internet service provider,services and gateways
*   broadband routing and performance monitoring
*   email and website services from internet providers
*   professional services to design, build and manage network connections

Expires: 17/07/2027

[44 suppliers](https://www.gca.gov.uk/agreements/RM6116:1a/lot-suppliers)

Lot 1b: Commercial Radio Capabilities

Voice communication systems using ultra/very high frequency radio technology. This includes but is not limited to:  

*   design, survey, build and installation services
*   secure radio and support equipment
*   mobile radio and two-way transceivers

## How to buy

There are 3 ways to buy from this agreement. These are direct award from a catalogue, further competition, or aggregation.

### **Direct award**

*   available on all lots and suitable for straightforward, commoditised requirements
*   supplier offers are shown in the government marketplace
    *   if you currently use e-Marketplace you should already be able to access the catalogue

### **Further competition**

*   use for all your requirements
*   can be used when you require services or products from multiple lots
*   should be used when you need suppliers to develop proposals or solutions to meet your statement of requirements
*   further competition helps you to amend or refine a wider range of the template call-off terms and conditions, giving you more flexibility when defining your statement of requirements

### Aggregation

*   we use our complementary [aggregation](https://www.gca.gov.uk/products-and-services/aggregation) service to bring together customers with similar requirements
*   we leverage the volume to create greater commercial benefits for customers
*   we manage the procurement process from start to finish
*   case studies on successful aggregations are available to download below

[Email the team for more information](mailto:aggregation@gca.gov.uk).

For a more detailed step-by-step process on how to run a direct award or further competition, download the buyer guide in the documents section below.

# Network Services 3

UK public sector organisations can access network solutions and communication services. This includes cloud connectivity, audio and video conferencing, radio and satellite networking, and emerging technologies like Smart Cities. 

## Updates

**15 August 2025:** This framework was set up under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015. These rules still apply for the full agreement. Both buying methods (further competition and direct award) remain available, even though the Procurement Act 2023 is now in effect.

**12 March 2025:** We have extended the length of this agreement by 24 months. The new end date is 17 July 2027. The new end date for lots 1c and 1d is 22 May 2027.

**19 September 2024:** If you are buying connectivity services under lot 1a or 2a we have a new template and guidance video to help define your requirements:

*   [connectivity in a box template document This file will download](https://assets.crowncommercial.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/Connectivity-In-A-Box-Template-v3-1.ods)
*   [connectivity in a box guidance video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZQT815Vf7-M)

**20 September 2023:** Mobile voice and data services are no longer part of this framework. Use the new [RM6261 Mobile Voice and Data Services Framework instead.](https://www.gca.gov.uk/agreements/RM6261)

**28 July 2023:**[Watch our RM6116 customer webinar.](https://youtu.be/NjFoaPzUZBU) It provides information on:

*   framework overview
*   buying process (direct award and further competition)
*   terms and conditions and service offers

## Description

Provides you with the flexibility to update, improve or simplify your network systems. Services and products you can buy include:

*   **routers, switches and cables:** equipment which allows network access
*   **local area networks:** equipment which allows connectivity within your organisation’s premises
*   internet access and fibre optic cabling
*   5G networks
*   **Internet Protocol (IP) telephony:** voice calls over the internet
*   **cloud services:**internet-based computing such as servers, storage and databases
*   **collaboration solutions:** audio and video conferencing
*   **unified communications:** platforms or applications that combine communication methods including voice, video and data services
*   **satellite networking:** wireless communication that uses satellites to send data and provide internet connectivity
*   maintenance and support services
*   **contact centre services:** software that connects many communication channels such as voice, email, chat and social media into a single unified system
*   security and surveillance
*   **professional services:** design, install and manage network solutions

### **Emerging technologies**

The agreement also includes access to newer technologies:

*   Internet of Things (IoT) and Smart Technologies (smart, shared, connected spaces)
*   tactical radio services (secure communication systems in high-risk unpredictable environments)
*   critical domain services (register and manage domain names)
*   communication platform as a service (embed real-time communication features into your own systems)

You can buy complete managed solutions from a single supplier. Or you can buy individual parts as needed. This helps you modernise, optimise, and simplify your network for hybrid working.

### **Agreement length**

Network services 3 will run for 2 years, with 2 optional 12-month extensions.

## Benefits

*   provides a complete range of network services from network infrastructure to fully integrated communication suites
*   introduces emerging technologies that reflect changes in the marketplace and future consumption of network solutions
*   supports the government’s “cloud first” initiatives aimed at enabling public internet connectivity solutions, and migration off the Public Sector Network (PSN)
*   attracts solution providers, service integrators and managed service providers who can remove the complexity of design from the end-user, and design, build and deliver solutions that provide cost and network optimisation
*   providing a WAN/LAN RFQ template to enable more “further competition” on public internet connectivity solutions and ultimately provide customers with better value for money
*   enabling direct awards on all Lots for commoditised procurements
*   enabling cross-lot competitions where managed services span across more than one capability

### Carbon Reduction

All suppliers have committed to comply with Procurement Policy Note 006, ['Taking account of Carbon Reduction Plans in the procurement of major government contracts'](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ppn-006-taking-account-of-carbon-reduction-plans-in-the-procurement-of-major-government-contracts) as required. If a supplier is required to publish a carbon reduction plan, you can find it on their individual supplier details page.

## How to buy

There are 3 ways to buy from this agreement. These are direct award from a catalogue, further competition, or aggregation.

### **Direct award**

*   available on all lots and suitable for straightforward, commoditised requirements
*   supplier offers are shown in the government marketplace
    *   if you currently use e-Marketplace you should already be able to access the catalogue

### **Further competition**

*   use for all your requirements
*   can be used when you require services or products from multiple lots
*   should be used when you need suppliers to develop proposals or solutions to meet your statement of requirements
*   further competition helps you to amend or refine a wider range of the template call-off terms and conditions, giving you more flexibility when defining your statement of requirements

### Aggregation

*   we use our complementary [aggregation](https://www.gca.gov.uk/products-and-services/aggregation) service to bring together customers with similar requirements
*   we leverage the volume to create greater commercial benefits for customers
*   we manage the procurement process from start to finish
*   case studies on successful aggregations are available to download below

[Email the team for more information](mailto:aggregation@gca.gov.uk).

For a more detailed step-by-step process on how to run a direct award or further competition, download the buyer guide in the documents section below.

# The Complete Guide to Framework Agreements in Public Procurement

![Image 1: hero-image](https://res.cloudinary.com/du0fs5dsp/image/upload/c_limit,w_3840/f_auto/q_auto/v1/22_oqob6u?_a=BAVMn6DW0)

Framework agreements are one of the most powerful tools in public procurement - but also among the most misunderstood.

For suppliers, they represent a unique chance to unlock long-term, recurring business with public buyers. For buyers, they offer speed, flexibility, and compliance in a single procurement model.

And yet, many businesses don’t fully understand what frameworks are, how to get on them, or how to win once they’re in.

This guide cuts through the complexity. Whether you're an SME [bidding](https://info.mercell.com/en/procurement-insights/what-is-public-bidding/) for your first framework or a seasoned supplier refining your strategy, you’ll find clear, actionable insights to help you compete and succeed - every step of the way.

In this guide, you'll learn:

*   What a framework agreement is and how it works

*   The different types of frameworks and their advantages

*   How to find, prepare for, and win a place on a framework

*   What buyers look for - and how to stand out

*   How to manage your position once awarded

## What Is a Framework Agreement?

A framework agreement is a long-term contract between one or more [public sector](https://info.mercell.com/en/blog/what-is-public-sector/) buyers and one or more suppliers. Instead of buying goods or services outright, the buyer sets up a framework that outlines the terms - pricing, quality standards, delivery conditions, etc. - for future purchases over a set period (typically 2–4 years).

Crucially, a framework does not guarantee volume or exclusivity. It simply creates a structure for procurement, allowing purchases to be made as needed through call-offs or mini-competitions.

## How Framework Agreements Work

To fully understand the value of framework agreements, it helps to break down how they’re structured and what makes them different from standard contracts. These foundational elements define how suppliers are selected, how purchases are made, and what expectations are set on both sides.

*   Duration: Usually 2–4 years, with no extensions beyond 4 years unless justified. This fixed term provides suppliers with a stable, multi-year opportunity pipeline while ensuring buyers can adapt to market changes periodically.

*   Parties Involved: Can include a single buyer or a group of contracting authorities (e.g., central government, local councils). Frameworks set up by central bodies or consortia allow suppliers to access multiple buyers through one successful bid.

*   Multiple Suppliers: Often awarded to multiple suppliers to maintain competition throughout the life of the framework. This enables buyers to choose from a qualified pool based on performance, pricing, or suitability for a specific requirement.

*   No Guaranteed Spend: Being on a framework offers opportunity, not certainty - buyers are not obligated to place orders. Suppliers must remain proactive, responsive, and competitive to win business through mini-competitions or direct awards.

## Types of Framework Agreements

There are two common forms:

### 1. Single-Supplier Framework

Only one supplier is appointed. All orders during the contract term are made with that supplier. These are more common for highly specialized or niche services.

### 2. Multi-Supplier Framework

Several suppliers are appointed. Buyers can either:

*   Direct award a contract based on pre-agreed terms (e.g. best price), or

*   Run a mini-competition between framework participants to ensure value and fit for a specific need.

This flexibility makes multi-supplier frameworks especially attractive to buyers - but it also means the competition doesn't end when you're awarded a place. Suppliers must continue to demonstrate value throughout the framework's lifespan.

But before any of that happens, you need to earn your spot.

## How to Get on a Framework

Securing a place on a framework agreement is a high-value opportunity, but it’s also a competitive and often complex process. Public buyers use frameworks to pre-select suppliers who meet strict criteria - not just in pricing and capability, but in compliance, delivery, and long-term value.

Here’s how to give yourself the [best chance of winning](https://info.mercell.com/en/blog/how-to-write-winning-bids/ "how to write winning bids") a place on a framework:

### 1. Monitor and Identify Relevant Frameworks Early

Framework tenders are often announced well in advance of their start dates. Finding them early gives you more time to prepare, gather documentation, and align your team.

Use platforms like [Mercell](https://info.mercell.com/) to:

*   Track upcoming frameworks in your region and industry

*   [Monitor](https://info.mercell.com/en/procurement-insights/tender-monitoring-guide/) expiring frameworks so you’re ready to bid when they reopen

*   Discover multi-buyer frameworks that can give you access to a larger pool of potential clients

*   Set tailored alerts based on CPV codes, locations, and keywords to never miss a relevant opportunity

Pro tip: Build a pipeline of target frameworks 6–12 months in advance so you're not scrambling when the [tender](https://info.mercell.com/en/procurement-insights/what-is-public-tendering/) is published.

### 2. Assess Your Readiness to Compete

Frameworks often demand more than a standard bid. You’ll need to demonstrate your ability to deliver consistent value over multiple years, to multiple buyers, across different geographies or service lines.

Key readiness factors:

*   Capacity – Can you scale delivery if multiple buyers request your services at once?

*   Experience – Do you have past performance examples that match the scope and complexity of the framework?

*   Certifications – Are your legal, quality, data, and ESG certifications current and complete?

*   Financial stability – Are your accounts, insurances, and credit standing up to date?

Perform a gap analysis well before the tender to fix any shortcomings in your qualifications or documentation.

### 3. Understand the Tender Documentation in Detail

When the tender goes live, the buyer will typically publish a set of documents including:

*   Specification of services/goods

*   Qualification and selection criteria (SQ, ESPD)

*   Award criteria (e.g., 60% quality / 40% price)

*   Terms and conditions for the framework

*   Instructions for submission and deadlines

Don’t skim these - study them line by line. Create a summary sheet of key requirements and assign internal owners to each task (e.g., finance lead handles pricing, legal checks T&Cs, delivery team reviews scope).

Pro tip: Use bid management tools like Mercell Bidding to centralize these tasks, track deadlines, and avoid last-minute errors.

### 4. Craft a Targeted, High-Scoring Response

Your bid must be both technically sound and strategically sharp. You’re competing not just to meet the requirements - but to outperform every other supplier applying for the same slots.

Focus on these areas:

#### A) Tailored Technical Responses

*   Use the buyer’s language and address their specific outcomes

*   Include examples that mirror the framework’s expected delivery model

*   Show clear processes for onboarding, communication, quality control, and risk mitigation

#### B) Pricing Strategy

*   Be competitive, but sustainable - buyers can see through unrealistic pricing

*   Consider how your pricing will scale or vary across multiple buyers

*   Clearly explain any added value or optional services

#### C) Social Value and Innovation

*   Many frameworks include scoring for environmental, social, or community impact

*   Detail your sustainability credentials, inclusive hiring practices, or digital innovation

#### D) Consistency and Clarity

*   Use templates for formatting and branding

*   Cross-reference your answers with the evaluation criteria

*   Get a second set of eyes on everything before submission

Pro tip: Evaluate your own bid before submitting it using a mock scoring session against the published award criteria.

### 5. Prepare for Ongoing Framework Management

Winning a framework place is only the first step. Buyers want partners who can deliver smoothly, report transparently, and stay compliant over time.

If awarded a place:

*   Set up a framework onboarding process internally

*   Establish a named account lead and communication plan for each buyer

*   Maintain updated documents (e.g., insurances, certificates, policies)

*   [Prepare](https://info.mercell.com/en/procurement-insights/tender-preparations/) for mini-competitions with quick-turnaround bid templates

Frameworks are relationships. Treat them with the same level of attention and professionalism as you would your most valuable clients.

## Mini-Competitions: Where the Real Work Begins

Getting onto a framework is a major achievement - but it’s not the end of the journey. Most actual work is awarded through mini-competitions between approved suppliers. These are short, targeted bidding events where buyers invite multiple framework suppliers to propose specific solutions or pricing for a defined scope.

Buyers run mini-competitions to ensure continued value and flexibility within the framework. They may request updated pricing, refined delivery plans, or tailored approaches to a particular project or location. Deadlines are usually tight, and submissions must be clear, compliant, and highly responsive to the brief.

To stand out, suppliers need to be fast, organized, and relevant:

*   Have pre-approved response templates and pricing models ready

*   Assign a mini-competition team who can mobilize quickly

*   Focus on clarity, compliance, and any differentiators (speed, innovation, service model)

Tip: Tools like Mercell Bidding can streamline this process, helping teams collaborate, manage deadlines, and submit polished bids under pressure.

The most successful suppliers don’t just wait for opportunities - they’re always ready to respond, win, and deliver.

## Conclusion

Framework agreements are a strategic gateway to long-term public business. With the right preparation, insight, and positioning, a single framework can open doors to dozens of new buyers, consistent revenue, and lasting relationships.

But success doesn’t happen by accident. It requires early planning, strong bid writing, and a clear understanding of what buyers expect - not just today, but over the full life of the framework.

If you're serious about growing your public sector presence, frameworks aren’t optional - they're essential. And with the right strategy in place, your next win could be the one that transforms your business.

Ready to win your next framework?

# The Complete Guide to Framework Agreements in Public Procurement

![Image 1: hero-image](https://res.cloudinary.com/du0fs5dsp/image/upload/c_limit,w_3840/f_auto/q_auto/v1/22_oqob6u?_a=BAVMn6DW0)

Framework agreements are one of the most powerful tools in public procurement - but also among the most misunderstood.

For suppliers, they represent a unique chance to unlock long-term, recurring business with public buyers. For buyers, they offer speed, flexibility, and compliance in a single procurement model.

And yet, many businesses don’t fully understand what frameworks are, how to get on them, or how to win once they’re in.

This guide cuts through the complexity. Whether you're an SME [bidding](https://info.mercell.com/en/procurement-insights/what-is-public-bidding/) for your first framework or a seasoned supplier refining your strategy, you’ll find clear, actionable insights to help you compete and succeed - every step of the way.

In this guide, you'll learn:

*   What a framework agreement is and how it works

*   The different types of frameworks and their advantages

*   How to find, prepare for, and win a place on a framework

*   What buyers look for - and how to stand out

*   How to manage your position once awarded

## What Is a Framework Agreement?

A framework agreement is a long-term contract between one or more [public sector](https://info.mercell.com/en/blog/what-is-public-sector/) buyers and one or more suppliers. Instead of buying goods or services outright, the buyer sets up a framework that outlines the terms - pricing, quality standards, delivery conditions, etc. - for future purchases over a set period (typically 2–4 years).

Crucially, a framework does not guarantee volume or exclusivity. It simply creates a structure for procurement, allowing purchases to be made as needed through call-offs or mini-competitions.

## How Framework Agreements Work

To fully understand the value of framework agreements, it helps to break down how they’re structured and what makes them different from standard contracts. These foundational elements define how suppliers are selected, how purchases are made, and what expectations are set on both sides.

*   Duration: Usually 2–4 years, with no extensions beyond 4 years unless justified. This fixed term provides suppliers with a stable, multi-year opportunity pipeline while ensuring buyers can adapt to market changes periodically.

*   Parties Involved: Can include a single buyer or a group of contracting authorities (e.g., central government, local councils). Frameworks set up by central bodies or consortia allow suppliers to access multiple buyers through one successful bid.

*   Multiple Suppliers: Often awarded to multiple suppliers to maintain competition throughout the life of the framework. This enables buyers to choose from a qualified pool based on performance, pricing, or suitability for a specific requirement.

*   No Guaranteed Spend: Being on a framework offers opportunity, not certainty - buyers are not obligated to place orders. Suppliers must remain proactive, responsive, and competitive to win business through mini-competitions or direct awards.

## Types of Framework Agreements

There are two common forms:

### 1. Single-Supplier Framework

Only one supplier is appointed. All orders during the contract term are made with that supplier. These are more common for highly specialized or niche services.

### 2. Multi-Supplier Framework

Several suppliers are appointed. Buyers can either:

*   Direct award a contract based on pre-agreed terms (e.g. best price), or

*   Run a mini-competition between framework participants to ensure value and fit for a specific need.

This flexibility makes multi-supplier frameworks especially attractive to buyers - but it also means the competition doesn't end when you're awarded a place. Suppliers must continue to demonstrate value throughout the framework's lifespan.

But before any of that happens, you need to earn your spot.

## How to Get on a Framework

Securing a place on a framework agreement is a high-value opportunity, but it’s also a competitive and often complex process. Public buyers use frameworks to pre-select suppliers who meet strict criteria - not just in pricing and capability, but in compliance, delivery, and long-term value.

Here’s how to give yourself the [best chance of winning](https://info.mercell.com/en/blog/how-to-write-winning-bids/ "how to write winning bids") a place on a framework:

### 1. Monitor and Identify Relevant Frameworks Early

Framework tenders are often announced well in advance of their start dates. Finding them early gives you more time to prepare, gather documentation, and align your team.

Use platforms like [Mercell](https://info.mercell.com/) to:

*   Track upcoming frameworks in your region and industry

*   [Monitor](https://info.mercell.com/en/procurement-insights/tender-monitoring-guide/) expiring frameworks so you’re ready to bid when they reopen

*   Discover multi-buyer frameworks that can give you access to a larger pool of potential clients

*   Set tailored alerts based on CPV codes, locations, and keywords to never miss a relevant opportunity

Pro tip: Build a pipeline of target frameworks 6–12 months in advance so you're not scrambling when the [tender](https://info.mercell.com/en/procurement-insights/what-is-public-tendering/) is published.

### 2. Assess Your Readiness to Compete

Frameworks often demand more than a standard bid. You’ll need to demonstrate your ability to deliver consistent value over multiple years, to multiple buyers, across different geographies or service lines.

Key readiness factors:

*   Capacity – Can you scale delivery if multiple buyers request your services at once?

*   Experience – Do you have past performance examples that match the scope and complexity of the framework?

*   Certifications – Are your legal, quality, data, and ESG certifications current and complete?

*   Financial stability – Are your accounts, insurances, and credit standing up to date?

Perform a gap analysis well before the tender to fix any shortcomings in your qualifications or documentation.

### 3. Understand the Tender Documentation in Detail

When the tender goes live, the buyer will typically publish a set of documents including:

*   Specification of services/goods

*   Qualification and selection criteria (SQ, ESPD)

*   Award criteria (e.g., 60% quality / 40% price)

*   Terms and conditions for the framework

*   Instructions for submission and deadlines

Don’t skim these - study them line by line. Create a summary sheet of key requirements and assign internal owners to each task (e.g., finance lead handles pricing, legal checks T&Cs, delivery team reviews scope).

Pro tip: Use bid management tools like Mercell Bidding to centralize these tasks, track deadlines, and avoid last-minute errors.

### 4. Craft a Targeted, High-Scoring Response

Your bid must be both technically sound and strategically sharp. You’re competing not just to meet the requirements - but to outperform every other supplier applying for the same slots.

Focus on these areas:

#### A) Tailored Technical Responses

*   Use the buyer’s language and address their specific outcomes

*   Include examples that mirror the framework’s expected delivery model

*   Show clear processes for onboarding, communication, quality control, and risk mitigation

#### B) Pricing Strategy

*   Be competitive, but sustainable - buyers can see through unrealistic pricing

*   Consider how your pricing will scale or vary across multiple buyers

*   Clearly explain any added value or optional services

#### C) Social Value and Innovation

*   Many frameworks include scoring for environmental, social, or community impact

*   Detail your sustainability credentials, inclusive hiring practices, or digital innovation

#### D) Consistency and Clarity

*   Use templates for formatting and branding

*   Cross-reference your answers with the evaluation criteria

*   Get a second set of eyes on everything before submission

Pro tip: Evaluate your own bid before submitting it using a mock scoring session against the published award criteria.

### 5. Prepare for Ongoing Framework Management

Winning a framework place is only the first step. Buyers want partners who can deliver smoothly, report transparently, and stay compliant over time.

If awarded a place:

*   Set up a framework onboarding process internally

*   Establish a named account lead and communication plan for each buyer

*   Maintain updated documents (e.g., insurances, certificates, policies)

*   [Prepare](https://info.mercell.com/en/procurement-insights/tender-preparations/) for mini-competitions with quick-turnaround bid templates

Frameworks are relationships. Treat them with the same level of attention and professionalism as you would your most valuable clients.

## Mini-Competitions: Where the Real Work Begins

Getting onto a framework is a major achievement - but it’s not the end of the journey. Most actual work is awarded through mini-competitions between approved suppliers. These are short, targeted bidding events where buyers invite multiple framework suppliers to propose specific solutions or pricing for a defined scope.

Buyers run mini-competitions to ensure continued value and flexibility within the framework. They may request updated pricing, refined delivery plans, or tailored approaches to a particular project or location. Deadlines are usually tight, and submissions must be clear, compliant, and highly responsive to the brief.

To stand out, suppliers need to be fast, organized, and relevant:

*   Have pre-approved response templates and pricing models ready

*   Assign a mini-competition team who can mobilize quickly

*   Focus on clarity, compliance, and any differentiators (speed, innovation, service model)

Tip: Tools like Mercell Bidding can streamline this process, helping teams collaborate, manage deadlines, and submit polished bids under pressure.

The most successful suppliers don’t just wait for opportunities - they’re always ready to respond, win, and deliver.

## Conclusion

Framework agreements are a strategic gateway to long-term public business. With the right preparation, insight, and positioning, a single framework can open doors to dozens of new buyers, consistent revenue, and lasting relationships.

But success doesn’t happen by accident. It requires early planning, strong bid writing, and a clear understanding of what buyers expect - not just today, but over the full life of the framework.

If you're serious about growing your public sector presence, frameworks aren’t optional - they're essential. And with the right strategy in place, your next win could be the one that transforms your business.

L. No. 116-124, 133 Stat. 158 (2020) (codified as amended at 47 U.S.C. §§ 1601–1609). Pursuant to the Commission’s rules, the Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau will maintain this list on the Commission’s website, and will monitor the status of any determinations in order to update the Covered List. More information on how the Covered List is compiled and updated can be found in the Commission’s rules at 47 C.F.R.§ 1.50000 _et seq._

##### **Importation/Marketing Prohibitions on Previously-Authorized Covered Equipment**

In order to mitigate potential national security risks associated with covered equipment that was authorized prior to a Covered List addition under 47 U.S.C. § 1601(b), the Commission, in the [_EA Security Second Report and Order_](https://www.fcc.gov/document/fcc-approves-new-safeguards-against-untrustworthy-gear-0), created a process allowing PSHSB and OET, through delegated authority, to limit existing authorizations to stop further importation or marketing of covered equipment in order to mitigate national security risks. Under this process, codified at [47 CFR § 2.939(e)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-2/subpart-J/subject-group-ECFRd5ad3b739dbf27a/section-2.939), PSHSB and OET must issue a Public Notice identifying the affected equipment, provide at least 30 days for public comment, and conduct a public interest analysis before determining whether to apply such limitations. ### Importation/Marketing Prohibitions

(Updated September 18, 2026)

##### **Importation/Marketing Prohibitions on Previously-Authorized Covered Equipment**

In order to mitigate potential national security risks associated with covered equipment that was authorized prior to a Covered List addition under 47 U.S.C. § 1601(b), the Commission, in the [_EA Security Second Report and Order_](https://www.fcc.gov/document/fcc-approves-new-safeguards-against-untrustworthy-gear-0), created a process allowing PSHSB and OET, through delegated authority, to limit existing authorizations to stop further importation or marketing of covered equipment in order to mitigate national security risks. Under this process, codified at [47 CFR § 2.939(e)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-2/subpart-J/subject-group-ECFRd5ad3b739dbf27a/section-2.939), PSHSB and OET must issue a Public Notice identifying the affected equipment, provide at least 30 days for public comment, and conduct a public interest analysis before determining whether to apply such limitations. Below is the list of covered equipment subject to importation and/or marketing prohibitions.

# List of Equipment and Services Covered By Section 2 of The Secure Networks Act

## Frequently Asked Questions

*   [UAS and UAS Critical Components on the FCC Covered List](https://www.fcc.gov/covered-list-faqs-uas-and-uas-critical-components)
*   [Routers Produced in Foreign Countries](https://www.fcc.gov/faqs-recent-updates-fcc-covered-list-regarding-routers-produced-foreign-countries)
*   [Foreign-Produced Advanced Robotic Devices and Power Inverters](https://www.fcc.gov/covered-list-faqs-robots-inverters)

Section 1.50002 of the Commission’s rules directs the Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau to publish a list of communications equipment and services (Covered List) that are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons, based exclusively on any of four sources for such a determination and that such equipment or services possess certain capabilities as enumerated in section 2(a) of the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019, Pub. L. No. 116-124, 133 Stat. 158 (2020) (codified as amended at 47 U.S.C. §§ 1601–1609). Pursuant to the Commission’s rules, the Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau will maintain this list on the Commission’s website, and will monitor the status of any determinations in order to update the Covered List. More information on how the Covered List is compiled and updated can be found in the Commission’s rules at 47 C.F.R.§ 1.50000 _et seq._

##### **Importation/Marketing Prohibitions on Previously-Authorized Covered Equipment**

In order to mitigate potential national security risks associated with covered equipment that was authorized prior to a Covered List addition under 47 U.S.C. § 1601(b), the Commission, in the [_EA Security Second Report and Order_](https://www.fcc.gov/document/fcc-approves-new-safeguards-against-untrustworthy-gear-0), created a process allowing PSHSB and OET, through delegated authority, to limit existing authorizations to stop further importation or marketing of covered equipment in order to mitigate national security risks. Under this process, codified at [47 CFR § 2.939(e)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-2/subpart-J/subject-group-ECFRd5ad3b739dbf27a/section-2.939), PSHSB and OET must issue a Public Notice identifying the affected equipment, provide at least 30 days for public comment, and conduct a public interest analysis before determining whether to apply such limitations. ### Importation/Marketing Prohibitions

(Updated September 18, 2026)

##### **Importation/Marketing Prohibitions on Previously-Authorized Covered Equipment**

In order to mitigate potential national security risks associated with covered equipment that was authorized prior to a Covered List addition under 47 U.S.C. § 1601(b), the Commission, in the [_EA Security Second Report and Order_](https://www.fcc.gov/document/fcc-approves-new-safeguards-against-untrustworthy-gear-0), created a process allowing PSHSB and OET, through delegated authority, to limit existing authorizations to stop further importation or marketing of covered equipment in order to mitigate national security risks. Under this process, codified at [47 CFR § 2.939(e)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-2/subpart-J/subject-group-ECFRd5ad3b739dbf27a/section-2.939), PSHSB and OET must issue a Public Notice identifying the affected equipment, provide at least 30 days for public comment, and conduct a public interest analysis before determining whether to apply such limitations. Below is the list of covered equipment subject to importation and/or marketing prohibitions.

# Supply Chain and Technology Agreements in Data Center Construction: Navigating Component Shortages and Alternative Sourcing

    *   [](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Supply%20Chain%20and%20Technology%20Agreements%20in%20Data%20Center%20Construction%3A%20Navigating%20Component%20Shortages%20and%20Alternative%20Sourcing&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bracewell.com%2Fresources%2Fdata-center-supply-chain-and-technology-agreements%2F "Share Supply Chain and Technology Agreements in Data Center Construction: Navigating Component Shortages and Alternative Sourcing on Twitter")

 January 26, 2026 |6 minute read

Data centers are the backbone of today’s digital economy and are even more important to its future, powering everything from cloud services to ever increasing AI-driven applications. To address this demand, the development and construction of data centers is proceeding at an extremely fast pace, with numerous investors and parties searching for suitable land, acquiring that land, and then trying to commence construction as quickly as possible.

However, building these facilities is no small feat – especially when global supply chain disruptions, caused in part be the increased demand for these facilities, threaten the availability of critical components like electronic components, servers, batteries, cooling systems and networking gear.

To mitigate these risks, data center operators are increasingly relying on robust **supply chain and technology agreements** that include **component shortage remedies**, **price adjustment clauses**,**alternative sourcing clauses**as well as**revamped force majeure**and**liquidated damage clauses**. These contractual tools help ensure project continuity, provide confidence to lenders, control costs and provide operational resilience. Because these contracts often limit consequential damage, it is imperative to consider these issues.

In this Q&A, we explore the most pressing questions surrounding these agreements and how they safeguard data center construction projects.

## **1. Why Are Data Center Supply Chain Agreements Critical?**

Data center supply chain agreements form the foundation for timely procurement and delivery of essential hardware and technology components for data center construction so that delays and increased costs can be avoided. Because data center projects are in such high demand and often have aggressive lending facilities, the development of these centers are on tight schedules, and delays can lead to serious challenges that threaten to scuttle projects – such as increased costs, missed service-level commitments and market irrelevance, and the triggering of unwanted debt remedies.

While these agreements are not a magic bullet that eliminates these risks, they can minimize delays and disruptions and control expectations by defining delivery timelines, setting forth quality standards and contingency measures, provide alternatives and remedies when supply chain disruptions are unavoidable, and ensure that all parties understand their obligations and remedies in case of disruptions.

## **2. What Causes Component Shortages in Data Center Projects?**

Component shortages in data center projects can be caused by many issues, including but not limited to:

*   increased global demand for specific components needed for AI infrastructures
*   deficiencies in supply sometimes associated with newer and/or higher-performing technologies that are not as easy to produce
*   increased tariffs on certain countries or products, global semiconductor constraints
*   geopolitical trade disruptions, political instability in certain regions
*   war, pandemics, extreme weather events and disasters and transportation bottlenecks that delay critical deliveries

While these shortages can sometimes be foreseeable and of limited length, they can sometimes be unpredictable and indefinite.

## **3. How Can Technology Supply Agreements Address Component Shortages in Data Center Construction Projects?**

Data center technology supply agreements typically include **shortage remedy provisions** that:

*   prioritize allocation for critical projects, provide for cost allocation or sharing if there are substantial increases in costs
*   allow for the modification of normal supply and procurement procedures
*   set forth alternate products and sources
*   mandate expedited shipping procedures
*   require suppliers to maintain buffer inventories (and audit procedures to confirm such inventories)

These agreements can also provide streamlined termination procedures at low cost upon the triggering of certain metrics which may allow a contractor or operator to quickly obtain a new supplier or vendor. These clauses may also include escalation protocols, ensuring that shortages are addressed at senior management levels quickly.

By embedding these remedies into contracts, data center operators can reduce uncertainty and maintain construction momentum even during global supply chain turbulence.

## **4. What Is an Alternative Sourcing Clause?**

An **alternative sourcing clause** provides an option for operators or contractors to procure alternate components from secondary suppliers if the primary vendor fails to meet agreed delivery timelines. These are often triggered by certain metrics that are tied to reputable market indexes and/or more specific shortfalls that can be easily verified.

This flexibility is crucial in avoiding project delays. However, these clauses must clearly define what constitutes “equivalent” in terms of technical specifications, performance standards, and compliance requirements to prevent integration issues later.

## **5. How Do Alternative Sourcing Clauses Protect Data Center Project Timelines?**

Alternative sourcing clauses act as a safety net, allowing procurement teams to pivot quickly at reasonable costs without breaching contractual obligations. They also provide clarity to all parties involved so there are not any surprises that can create or foster legal disputes and delays.

Alternative sourcing clauses place competitive pressure on primary suppliers to adhere to timelines, knowing that buyers have clearly outlined contractual and legal alternatives and remedies. The combined effect of risk mitigation, performance incentives and clarifying alternatives and remedies with your supplier – makes these clauses imperative for owners, developers and contractors involved in data center construction projects.

## **6. Are There Downsides to Alternative Sourcing Clauses?**

While alternative sourcing offers flexibility, it introduces risks such as compatibility challenges, warranty limitations, and integration delays. For instance, a substitute cooling system may meet technical specs but require additional engineering work to fit existing designs.

To mitigate these risks, data center construction agreements should mandate supplier cooperation during transitions and include provisions for technical validation before deployment.Though pushing for alternative sourcing clauses can also lead to a more adversarial negotiation process with your suppliers – which can cause delays in the execution of contracts – it is better to tolerate a painful negotiation on the front end of a project than have to deal with supply chain issues or legal actions during the project.

## **7. How Should Shortage Remedies Be Structured in Data Center Construction Agreements?**

Effective **shortage remedies** go beyond vague commitments and ambiguous language in your contract. They should be triggered by clear and specific metrics that are easily verifiable, with procedures and processes to implement those remedies. Effective shortage remedies should include:

*   **priority allocation** for critical projects during shortages
*   **escalation procedures** that trigger prompt senior-level intervention
*   **liquidated damages or credits** for missed delivery milestones
*   **access to inventory data and audits** for transparency and proactive planning
*   **price allocation mechanisms**to address unavoidable increases in products and materials
*   **reasonable termination procedures**and the relaxation of exclusivity requirements that are triggered by verifiable metrics or trusted indexes

These measures ensure accountability and provide buyers with actionable levers during crises.

## **8. Are There Financial Implications for Invoking Alternative Sourcing Clauses?**

Yes. Alternative sourcing often involves higher procurement costs, expedited shipping fees and potential integration expenses. They can also lead to legal costs if the clause is determined to be vague or ambiguous, further necessitating very specific and concrete language (sometimes including examples) so all parties know where they stand upon certain events.

Data center construction contracts should clearly outline cost-sharing mechanisms – such as whether the supplier bears additional costs if delays trigger alternative sourcing. They can also include cost sharing mechanisms when costs increase beyond a trusted pricing index or other verifiable metric, and ceilings and caps for those cost sharing mechanisms. This clarity prevents disputes and ensures fair allocation of financial responsibility.

## **9. How Do Global Supply Chain Trends Influence Data Center Construction Contracts?**

Emerging trends like nearshoring, supplier diversification, inventory auditing, price allocation mechanisms and AI-driven demand forecasting are reshaping supply chain strategies in data center construction. It should be noted however, that when employing AI-driven demand forecasting tools, or other AI-driven tools, they should be accompanied by human verification and compliance procedures.

Data center operators are increasingly embedding flexibility for owners, developers and contractors into contracts to adapt to these trends. For example, clauses now often include provisions for regional sourcing or dynamic allocation based on predictive analytics, making agreements more resilient to global events that may create disruptions.

## **10. What Best Practices Should Companies Follow When Drafting Data Center Supply Chain and Technology Sourcing Agreements?**

The following best practices can help create data center construction agreements that are both robust and adaptable:

*   **define clear technical equivalence standards** to avoid ambiguity
*   **provide clear contractual language, mechanisms, remedies and processes**to deal with issues that have specific language and examples, so parties are on the same page
*   **include collaboration obligations** for smooth integration of alternative components
*   **set transparent escalation and approval workflows** for invoking remedies
*   **align clauses with broader risk management strategies**, ensuring consistency across procurement and legal frameworks
*   **focus on reviewing and negotiating**the most critical contractual provisions, such as indemnity clauses, damage limitations, termination or suspension rights, force majeure clauses, liquidated damages and warranties

## **Conclusion**

In a time where data centers fuel AI innovation and digital infrastructure, supply chain vulnerabilities and disruptions can derail even the best planned projects. By embedding precise shortage remedies, alternative sourcing clauses and verifiable metrics into technology agreements, owners, developers and contractors can minimize delays, control costs and maintain lender confidence. These tools not only address current challenges like semiconductor shortages, tariffs and geopolitical tensions but also adapt to emerging trends such as nearshoring and AI-driven forecasting.

​Stakeholders should prioritize clear language, technical equivalence standards, remedies, cost-sharing allocations and collaborative obligations during negotiations to transform potential risks into competitive advantages and limit disputes because of vague or ambiguous provisions. Forward-thinking contracts that are specific and clear ensure data center projects launch on time, scale efficiently and thrive amid uncertain economic and political events.

 January 26, 2026 |6 minute read

Data centers are the backbone of today’s digital economy and are even more important to its future, powering everything from cloud services to ever increasing AI-driven applications. To address this demand, the development and construction of data centers is proceeding at an extremely fast pace, with numerous investors and parties searching for suitable land, acquiring that land, and then trying to commence construction as quickly as possible.

However, building these facilities is no small feat – especially when global supply chain disruptions, caused in part be the increased demand for these facilities, threaten the availability of critical components like electronic components, servers, batteries, cooling systems and networking gear.

To mitigate these risks, data center operators are increasingly relying on robust **supply chain and technology agreements** that include **component shortage remedies**, **price adjustment clauses**,**alternative sourcing clauses**as well as**revamped force majeure**and**liquidated damage clauses**. These contractual tools help ensure project continuity, provide confidence to lenders, control costs and provide operational resilience. Because these contracts often limit consequential damage, it is imperative to consider these issues.

In this Q&A, we explore the most pressing questions surrounding these agreements and how they safeguard data center construction projects.

## **1. Why Are Data Center Supply Chain Agreements Critical?**

Data center supply chain agreements form the foundation for timely procurement and delivery of essential hardware and technology components for data center construction so that delays and increased costs can be avoided. Because data center projects are in such high demand and often have aggressive lending facilities, the development of these centers are on tight schedules, and delays can lead to serious challenges that threaten to scuttle projects – such as increased costs, missed service-level commitments and market irrelevance, and the triggering of unwanted debt remedies.

While these agreements are not a magic bullet that eliminates these risks, they can minimize delays and disruptions and control expectations by defining delivery timelines, setting forth quality standards and contingency measures, provide alternatives and remedies when supply chain disruptions are unavoidable, and ensure that all parties understand their obligations and remedies in case of disruptions.

## **2. What Causes Component Shortages in Data Center Projects?**

Component shortages in data center projects can be caused by many issues, including but not limited to:

*   increased global demand for specific components needed for AI infrastructures
*   deficiencies in supply sometimes associated with newer and/or higher-performing technologies that are not as easy to produce
*   increased tariffs on certain countries or products, global semiconductor constraints
*   geopolitical trade disruptions, political instability in certain regions
*   war, pandemics, extreme weather events and disasters and transportation bottlenecks that delay critical deliveries

While these shortages can sometimes be foreseeable and of limited length, they can sometimes be unpredictable and indefinite.

## **3. How Can Technology Supply Agreements Address Component Shortages in Data Center Construction Projects?**

Data center technology supply agreements typically include **shortage remedy provisions** that:

*   prioritize allocation for critical projects, provide for cost allocation or sharing if there are substantial increases in costs
*   allow for the modification of normal supply and procurement procedures
*   set forth alternate products and sources
*   mandate expedited shipping procedures
*   require suppliers to maintain buffer inventories (and audit procedures to confirm such inventories)

These agreements can also provide streamlined termination procedures at low cost upon the triggering of certain metrics which may allow a contractor or operator to quickly obtain a new supplier or vendor. These clauses may also include escalation protocols, ensuring that shortages are addressed at senior management levels quickly.

By embedding these remedies into contracts, data center operators can reduce uncertainty and maintain construction momentum even during global supply chain turbulence.

## **4. What Is an Alternative Sourcing Clause?**

An **alternative sourcing clause** provides an option for operators or contractors to procure alternate components from secondary suppliers if the primary vendor fails to meet agreed delivery timelines. These are often triggered by certain metrics that are tied to reputable market indexes and/or more specific shortfalls that can be easily verified.

This flexibility is crucial in avoiding project delays. However, these clauses must clearly define what constitutes “equivalent” in terms of technical specifications, performance standards, and compliance requirements to prevent integration issues later.

## **5. How Do Alternative Sourcing Clauses Protect Data Center Project Timelines?**

Alternative sourcing clauses act as a safety net, allowing procurement teams to pivot quickly at reasonable costs without breaching contractual obligations. They also provide clarity to all parties involved so there are not any surprises that can create or foster legal disputes and delays.

Alternative sourcing clauses place competitive pressure on primary suppliers to adhere to timelines, knowing that buyers have clearly outlined contractual and legal alternatives and remedies. The combined effect of risk mitigation, performance incentives and clarifying alternatives and remedies with your supplier – makes these clauses imperative for owners, developers and contractors involved in data center construction projects.

## **6. Are There Downsides to Alternative Sourcing Clauses?**

While alternative sourcing offers flexibility, it introduces risks such as compatibility challenges, warranty limitations, and integration delays. For instance, a substitute cooling system may meet technical specs but require additional engineering work to fit existing designs.

To mitigate these risks, data center construction agreements should mandate supplier cooperation during transitions and include provisions for technical validation before deployment.Though pushing for alternative sourcing clauses can also lead to a more adversarial negotiation process with your suppliers – which can cause delays in the execution of contracts – it is better to tolerate a painful negotiation on the front end of a project than have to deal with supply chain issues or legal actions during the project.

## **7. How Should Shortage Remedies Be Structured in Data Center Construction Agreements?**

Effective **shortage remedies** go beyond vague commitments and ambiguous language in your contract. They should be triggered by clear and specific metrics that are easily verifiable, with procedures and processes to implement those remedies. Effective shortage remedies should include:

*   **priority allocation** for critical projects during shortages
*   **escalation procedures** that trigger prompt senior-level intervention
*   **liquidated damages or credits** for missed delivery milestones
*   **access to inventory data and audits** for transparency and proactive planning
*   **price allocation mechanisms**to address unavoidable increases in products and materials
*   **reasonable termination procedures**and the relaxation of exclusivity requirements that are triggered by verifiable metrics or trusted indexes

These measures ensure accountability and provide buyers with actionable levers during crises.

## **8. Are There Financial Implications for Invoking Alternative Sourcing Clauses?**

Yes. Alternative sourcing often involves higher procurement costs, expedited shipping fees and potential integration expenses. They can also lead to legal costs if the clause is determined to be vague or ambiguous, further necessitating very specific and concrete language (sometimes including examples) so all parties know where they stand upon certain events.

Data center construction contracts should clearly outline cost-sharing mechanisms – such as whether the supplier bears additional costs if delays trigger alternative sourcing. They can also include cost sharing mechanisms when costs increase beyond a trusted pricing index or other verifiable metric, and ceilings and caps for those cost sharing mechanisms. This clarity prevents disputes and ensures fair allocation of financial responsibility.

## **9. How Do Global Supply Chain Trends Influence Data Center Construction Contracts?**

Emerging trends like nearshoring, supplier diversification, inventory auditing, price allocation mechanisms and AI-driven demand forecasting are reshaping supply chain strategies in data center construction. It should be noted however, that when employing AI-driven demand forecasting tools, or other AI-driven tools, they should be accompanied by human verification and compliance procedures.

Data center operators are increasingly embedding flexibility for owners, developers and contractors into contracts to adapt to these trends. For example, clauses now often include provisions for regional sourcing or dynamic allocation based on predictive analytics, making agreements more resilient to global events that may create disruptions.

## **10. What Best Practices Should Companies Follow When Drafting Data Center Supply Chain and Technology Sourcing Agreements?**

The following best practices can help create data center construction agreements that are both robust and adaptable:

*   **define clear technical equivalence standards** to avoid ambiguity
*   **provide clear contractual language, mechanisms, remedies and processes**to deal with issues that have specific language and examples, so parties are on the same page
*   **include collaboration obligations** for smooth integration of alternative components
*   **set transparent escalation and approval workflows** for invoking remedies
*   **align clauses with broader risk management strategies**, ensuring consistency across procurement and legal frameworks
*   **focus on reviewing and negotiating**the most critical contractual provisions, such as indemnity clauses, damage limitations, termination or suspension rights, force majeure clauses, liquidated damages and warranties

## **Conclusion**

In a time where data centers fuel AI innovation and digital infrastructure, supply chain vulnerabilities and disruptions can derail even the best planned projects. By embedding precise shortage remedies, alternative sourcing clauses and verifiable metrics into technology agreements, owners, developers and contractors can minimize delays, control costs and maintain lender confidence. These tools not only address current challenges like semiconductor shortages, tariffs and geopolitical tensions but also adapt to emerging trends such as nearshoring and AI-driven forecasting.

​Stakeholders should prioritize clear language, technical equivalence standards, remedies, cost-sharing allocations and collaborative obligations during negotiations to transform potential risks into competitive advantages and limit disputes because of vague or ambiguous provisions. Forward-thinking contracts that are specific and clear ensure data center projects launch on time, scale efficiently and thrive amid uncertain economic and political events.

RE: FAR Case 2019-009, Prohibition on Contracting with Entities Using Certain
Telecommunications and Video Surveillance Services or Equipment

On behalf of the undersigned associations of the Council of Defense and Space
Industry Associations (CODSIA)1, we are pleased to submit these comments on the
interim FAR rule implementing Sec. 889(a)(1)(B) of the John S. McCain National
Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for Fiscal Year (FY) 2019, which prohibits
government agencies from contracting with entities that use telecommunications and
certain video surveillance equipment and services from five named entities2, as
published in the July 14, 2020 Federal Register3.

The CODSIA member associations wholeheartedly support the U.S. government’s goal
of preventing the exfiltration of sensitive information. Our member companies partner
directly with the Federal government to provide products and services intended to build
the U.S.’s technological capabilities against its adversaries and equip the warfighter. We
understand the inherent challenges that come with implementing a law as far-reaching
as Sec. 889 and also appreciate the inclusion of the new term “reasonable inquiry” as a
means of reducing the burden on contractors as they complete the law’s required
representation. Nonetheless, given the complex and interconnected nature of Federal
supply chain acquisition risk management policies and regulations, many aspects of the
interim rule require further elaboration and definition to help contractors ensure they can

Align Representation Requirements with Statutory Language

FAR 52.204-24(d)(2) has been amended as follows to implement the Sec. 889(a)(1)(B)
representation requirement:

“Offeror represents that— It [ ] does, [ ] does not  use covered telecommunications
equipment or services, or use any equipment, system, or service that uses covered
telecommunications equipment or services. The Offeror shall provide the additional
disclosure information required at paragraph (e)(2) of this section if the Offeror responds
‘‘does’’ in paragraph (d)(2) of this section.” [Emphasis added].

This representation language diverges from the language of the statute by its use of the
term “any” as highlighted above and its omission of the important qualifying language of
the statute. The statute provides explicit limiting language by applying the prohibition
only to use as a “substantial or essential” component of a system or as an item of
“critical technology” in a system as so designated by the government. The broad
language of the interim rule is not only divergent from the statutory text, but as drafted it
conflicts with the reasonable inquiry requirement and the applicability of the rule only to
prime contractors articulated in the rulemaking. The FAR representation should instead
track directly to the language of the statute. We suggest that the FAR Council adopt the
following substitution, with emphasis added:

“Offeror represents that— It [ ] does, [ ] does not  use covered telecommunications
equipment or services, or use any equipment, system, or service that uses covered
telecommunications equipment or services as a substantial or essential component
of any system, or as critical technology as part of any system. The Offeror shall
provide the additional disclosure information required at paragraph (e)(2) of this section
if the Offeror responds ‘‘does’’ in paragraph (d)(2) of this section.”

Consistent with Sec. 889(a)(1)(B), the interim rule requires contractors to undertake a
“reasonable inquiry.” Contractors are best positioned to evaluate the information in their
possession about the use of covered equipment or services used by the contractor.
The same is true for contractors’ ability to determine if any such equipment or services
are either a substantial or essential component of any system used by the contractor or
are critical technology for any system they use. The apparent shifting of this
assessment to contracting officers requires agencies to assess and understand
equipment systems or services used by the contractor. This apparent shift will result in

Provide Consistent Agency Interpretation and Application of the Rule

We recommend providing additional clarity to ensure that agencies do not have differing
interpretations of the rule’s application and its requirements. While we understand each
agency has a distinct risk profile and mission needs, drafting and enforcing uniform
guidance for agencies will ensure the quickest possible contractor delivery of innovative
products and minimize the disruption to government contracting brought on by the
statute. This is especially crucial when considering the volume of transactions occurring
through the various Government-wide Acquisition Contracts (GWACs) and GSA’s
implementation of the Cross-Agency Priority Goal on Sharing Quality Services; the
shifting focus on leveraging shared services across multiple agencies necessitates
better inter-agency coordination and consistent agency implementation and application
of a government-wide procurement regulation of this magnitude. However, agencies’
implementation should not be inconsistent with the interim rule’s direction on
applicability. Unfortunately, some agencies appear to be implementing the interim rule
in a manner inconsistent with the interim rule’s clear direction.

Our membership has reported that, beginning August 11, 2020, agencies have notified
contractors of their intention to issue unilateral changes to existing contracts, some with
contract modifications expected as late as October 2020, but with effective dates
retroactive to August 13, 2020. These “notifications” require representations with
language excerpted from FAR 52.204-24 that the contractor “does not use any

Clarify the Applicability of the ‘Part A’ and ‘Part B’ Prohibitions

Sec. 889 (a)(1)(A) and Sec. 889(a)(1)(B), while related, regulate different prohibited
activity. Accordingly, the final rule should separate the representations concerning Sec.
889(a)(1)(A) and Sec. 889(a)(1)(B), which not only regulate different prohibited activity,
but also require a different level of inquiry, including a flowdown obligation under Sec.
889(a)(1)(A), prior to providing a representation, into separate FAR provisions. As
federal agencies have implemented the Sec. 889(a)(1)(B) prohibition, there has been
considerable confusion and disruption as there are cases in which contracts have been
modified to incorporate the Sec. 889(a)(1)(B) prohibition, but have also incorporated the
Sec. 889(a)(1)(A) prohibition where it is not applicable, such as cases where products
have already been delivered under the contract. Such an inclusion would require the
contractor to submit a change proposal in order to recover costs associated with flowing
the Sec. 889(a)(1)(A) prohibition through the supply chain and the costs and delay
impacts associated with any potential redesign efforts. Separating  these prohibitions
into distinct FAR provisions will help clarify the appropriate respective applications and
prevent such situations.

would take effect August 13, 2021. There are several issues with this possible
expansion of Sec. 889(a)(1)(B)’s scope. First, the plain language of Sec. 889(a)(1)(B)
prohibits the government from contracting with “an entity that uses” covered
telecommunications equipment or services—t  here is nothing tying the prohibition to

Exclude Commercial Customers from the Rule’s Application

The use of covered telecommunications equipment or services by a commercial
customer of an entity should not be considered “use” of covered telecommunications
equipment or services by that entity for the purposes of determining compliance with
Sec. 889(a)(1)(B). Consistent with the current scope of the rule, which extends to the
entity executing the contract with a government agency, the rule should be limited to
procurement decisions over which the contracting entity has control. More specifically, a
contracting entity should not be responsible for—or required to make any inquiry into—a
decision to utilize covered equipment that is made by a customer with which the
contracting entity has a commercial relationship. Otherwise, contractors would be forced
to choose between meeting the new government-specific requirements and remaining
competitive in the global market.

For instance, consider the example of a contractor’s provision of IT services to a
commercial customer that requires the contractor to access the customer’s internal
telecommunications network or security systems that include covered equipment. The
contractor has no control over the customer’s procurement or use of the covered

Clarify That the Rule Does Not Apply to Backhaul, Roaming, and Interconnection
Agreements

Sec. 889(a)(2)(A) provides that the prohibitions in Sec. 889 do not “prohibit the head of
an executive agency from procuring with an entity to provide a service that connects to
the facilities of a third-party, such as backhaul, roaming or interconnection
arrangements.” The drafters of the interim rule interpret this provision to permit the
government to buy a service that connects to third-party backhaul—presumably, even
when covered telecommunications equipment is used in a backhaul. The commentary
states that the exception “applies only to a Government agency that is contracting with
an entity to provide a service.” Yet, the drafters also interpret the exception to mean that
the government may not (without a waiver) contract with a contractor that uses covered
telecommunications equipment or services to obtain backhaul services from an internet
service provider. The commentary says that the exception “does not apply to a
contractor’s use of a service that connects to the facilities of a third-party, such as
backhaul.”

This commentary has created significant confusion for contractors. In one instance, it
seems that a government agency does not need a waiver to contract for services
connecting to government networks to third-party backhaul containing covered
telecommunications equipment. But, at the same time, an executive agency would need
a waiver to contract with a supplier that relies on a third-party telecommunications
services provider whose network contains backhaul with covered telecommunications
equipment. If our reading of the commentary is accurate, the drafters are applying a
more restrictive standard to contracts that would not involve connecting government
networks to third-party backhaul containing covered telecommunications equipment
than they are to contracts that would connect government networks to such backhaul.
This outcome seems to be at odds with the purpose of the statutory exception—namely,
excluding third-party backhaul (and roaming and interconnection agreements) from the
scope of Sec. 889’s prohibitions.

Limit the Rule’s Application to Domestic Use of Covered Equipment

The interim rule contains a single scenario that is referenced in multiple locations in the
rule to the offering entity’s international operations. For instance, during the discussion
of the costs associated with this rule, the background information includes as an
example the possibility of an offering entity having to relocate a building in a foreign
country where there is no market alternative. The background information on the rule
also includes this specific question: “What do companies do if their factory or office is
located in a foreign country where covered telecommunications equipment or services
are prevalent and alternative solutions may be unavailable?” In those cases where the
rule applies to a building of a domestic concern that is covered under the rule, located in
a foreign country, the domestic concern would either seek a waiver or determine if there
is a technical solution or other option available that would result in eliminating the
covered use. A more efficient option, however, would be to limit the rule’s applicability to
covered equipment used in domestic offices of domestic concerns or, at a minimum, to
significantly streamline the waiver process for covered equipment used in domestic
concerns’ foreign offices where no viable local alternatives exist. The Director of
National Intelligence’s August 12, 2020 waiver granted to USAID for
telecommunications and internet services addresses this situation.4

A domestic concern’s overseas facilities likely depend on the use of covered prohibited
equipment at some point in their network. Such facilities use foreign carriers that could
have covered equipment installed. It would be incongruent to say that a government
facility’s carrier can have covered equipment, but a business’s overseas carrier cannot.
